Society & Human Rights
• UN reports five women were killed every hour in 2025 by partners or relatives, underscoring persistent gender-based violence. 
• An AP investigation alleges the US DEA allowed 1.4m fentanyl pills to be trafficked during a New Mexico sting, raising oversight concerns. 
• In DR Congo, residents filed a landmark suit alleging a Chinese-owned copper/cobalt mine caused severe pollution and health harms. 
• UK police arrested two after a suspected break‑in at Prince William and Catherine’s Sandringham residence; Millwall were penalised for discriminatory fan chants. 
• Immigration flashpoints: an Indian activist said his passport was flagged preventing UK travel, and a US-based scientist described arrest by ICE despite valid documents; Russia detained a regional governor in a rare elite crackdown. 
Why it matters: Rights, security and accountability pressures are intensifying across policing, immigration, gender violence and governance.

Armed Conflict & Security
• Ukraine’s war at sea expanded with a Russian warship sunk in Benghazi and strikes on cargo ships, while Russian missiles landing in Poland heightened NATO concern. 
• UK and US supply risks: MI5 warned of Russian sabotage against UK suppliers to Ukraine; the UK reportedly bought fake C4 for Kyiv; the Pentagon delayed Patriot interceptor deliveries. 
• DR Congo reported a missing military aircraft as rebels claimed a shootdown; a car bomb in a Colombian city wounded 20+; Syria’s landmine casualties are surging postwar. 
• Israel said it killed Hamas’s internal security chief in Gaza; settler arsons in the West Bank fuelled debate over “Jewish terrorism.” 
• NATO’s chief vowed defenses against space threats amid reports Russia could launch a nuclear warhead into orbit. 
Why it matters: The conflict map is widening and deepening, stressing alliances, supply chains and deterrence in Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

• CRE stress persists: an unprecedented CMBS wipeout will fully impair bonds backed by two Portland Hiltons. 
Why it matters: Markets are repricing AI exuberance amid governance and policy risks, while energy and credit stresses complicate the macro outlook.

Why it matters: Power politics, trade rules and tech governance are increasingly intertwined, reshaping alliances and corporate risk.

Climate & Environment
• COP31 collapsed without a pact; analyses urge learning from failure, while tracking outcomes on food, forests, oceans and nature. 
• England recorded a provisional record 5,258 heat‑related deaths in 2026; UK ministers face backlash over exempting most brownfield housing sites from biodiversity net gain rules. 
• AI data centers’ soaring electricity needs are complicating decarbonisation plans. 
• Conservation advances and alarms: Colombia’s frailejón “water guardians” scale up replanting; decades of citizen science reveal widespread declines in native Japanese plants; near‑surface Antarctic ice may hold ancient climate clues. 
• Volcanic activity reshaped Iwo Jima’s coastline, underscoring rapid geomorphic change. 
Why it matters: Policy gridlock collides with worsening impacts and new energy demands, even as science and citizen action provide tools and warnings.

Artificial Intelligence
• Nvidia’s leadership saga continues to reverberate: deepfakes proliferate, critics decry political interference, and employees welcomed Jensen Huang’s return as governance scrutiny intensifies. 
• Anthropic launched Claude Ship to review, fix and approve code; states sued SpaceX to stop Grok from generating CSAM; Amazon warned AI agents exploited a 0‑day with minimal human input. 
• Platforms tightened AI integration and controls: Meta brought Muse into Instagram DMs; Pinterest added parental limits on AI‑generated content. 
• Researchers and journals called for curbing AI “slop” without chilling legitimate work and urged humility on AI consciousness; reports touted AI‑assisted breakthroughs in major math problems. 
• Enterprise networks strain under AI loads; Amazon’s Decart acquisition aims to boost Trainium efficiency; OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo to secure Linux runtimes. 
Why it matters: Rapid AI deployment is colliding with safety, governance and infrastructure constraints, forcing faster policy and technical responses.

• An oral immune‑modulating drug showed strong efficacy and safety for moderate‑to‑severe eczema in a clinical trial.

Why it matters: Targeting microbiome chemistry, early neurodegeneration markers and nerve aging pathways could extend healthy lifespan and delay disease.

Art & Culture.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Masterpiece Commands a Record-Breaking $12.7 Million USD at Auction
Art & Culture.text: SummaryA 1920 abstract painting by pioneering artist Hilma af Klint recently sold for a record-breaking $12.7 million USD at a Swedish auction houseThe rare offering of 'Ser III No. 5' marks a historic moment for the artist whose foundation typically keeps her work strictly off the marketThe unprecedented sale sparked controversy among art historians who argue the esoteric work was never intended for commercial consumptionPioneering artist Hilma af Klint has set a new posthumous record following the landmark sale of her 1920 abstraction, Ser III No. 5. Hosted by the Bukowskis auction house in Stockholm, the extremely rare market appearance resulted in a staggering $12.7 million USD final price, a sum roughly 15 times its initial high estimate of $800,000 USD.Held closely by a single unnamed family since 1995, the painting was originally acquired after the artist's foundation deaccessioned a small number of works. The sale adds a lucrative new chapter to af Klint's posthumous ascent. While the artist remained relatively obscure following her death in 1944, a series of blockbuster museum exhibitions in the 2010s—including a record-shattering 2018 showcase at the New York Guggenheim Museum—firmly repositioned her as a foundational inventor of European abstraction. Her enigmatic canvases, featuring dazzling arrays of curlicuing lines and inscrutable symbols, were famously created in response to spirits she contacted.Because the foundation generally restricts her artwork from entering the commercial market, the recent Bukowskis auction sparked debate among art historians. Critics of the sale, including af Klint scholar Rachel Villari, argued that placing a price tag on the esoteric works contradicts the artist's original intentions and removes culturally significant pieces from public access. Despite the pushback, the auction house celebrated the historic hammer price, with CEO Louise Arén noting that simply selling an abstract work by af Klint is a remarkable feat on its own.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Climate & Environment.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
Climate & Environment.text: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into actionIn a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive. Continue reading...

Entertainment.title: Wynn Las Vegas Won Race Week
Entertainment.text: Formula 1 came back to Las Vegas for a fourth year, and the Grand Prix once again turned the Strip into a racetrack for a week. Most of the off-track action ended up at Wynn. Over five days, the resort hosted driver pop-ups, brand launches, panels, and club nights, and on Saturday night, it held the after-party everyone was trying to get into.That party was "The After", Zero Bond's Cadillac-presented event on Saturday, November 21, right after the checkered flag. Zero Bond, the private membership club Scott Sartiano and Will Makris started in New York, co-hosted with John Terzian and Brian Toll of The h.wood Group and Craig S. Billings of Wynn Las Vegas. Guests had signature cocktails and bites while H.E.R. played a live set. Later, Anderson .Paak took over as DJ Pee .Wee and kept the room going into the morning.The guest list read like a who's who of Race Week: Keegan-Michael Key, Ali Larter, Nina Dobrev, Damson Idris, Chace Crawford, Zack Bia, Bebe Rexha, Anthony Mackie, Eiza González, Alesso, Corey Gamble, Sophie Cunningham, Evan Ross, Iris Law, Jeff Ross, Jonathan Cheban, Madeline Fedyk, Jared Vanderbilt, Hannah Bronfman, Brendan Fallis, Dylan Efron and Charley Jordan.The drivers got there first. On Wednesday, Charles Leclerc opened Café Leclerc, his coffee pop-up, at Caffè Al Teatro and made an appearance in person. On Saturday, a few hours before the race, Lewis Hamilton stopped by his +44 pop-up on the Encore Esplanade.Friday had the fullest schedule. The Female Quotient and F1 ACADEMY held the FQ Lounge at Delilah, celebrating women breaking barriers in motorsport, with Susie Wolff and Nikki Fargas among the guests. Later that night, Olivia von Halle brought the loungewear label's exclusive Wynn capsule to Zero Bond with a pajama party co-hosted by Kelly Piquet. On Saturday, before the lights went out on the Strip, Zero Bond hosted one more event, this time for DIDRIS, Damson Idris' fine jewelry line.The late nights belonged to XS Nightclub, which reopened after a redesign. The Chainsmokers played Friday to a crowd that included Wiz Khalifa, Shaboozey, Landon Barker, Ashtin Earle, Keegan-Michael Key, Ty Dolla $ign, and Imagine Dragons' Dan Reynolds. On Saturday, Calvin Harris played for French Montana, Abla Sofy, Winnie Harlow, and Eiza González, and Alesso made a surprise appearance.Take a closer look at everything that went down at Wynn Las Vegas during race week in the gallery above.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Avengers, X-Men, and Fantastic Four Unite in the Final 'Avengers: Doomsday' Trailer
Entertainment.text: SummaryMarvel Studios has officially released the final trailer for its highly anticipated superhero blockbuster 'Avengers: Doomsday'The cinematic event introduces Robert Downey Jr. as the fearsome Doctor Doom while bringing back Chris Evans as Steve RogersDirected by Joe and Anthony Russo, the unprecedented crossover film officially hits theaters everywhere on December 18Marvel Studios has officially debuted the final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday. With less than a month remaining until the highly anticipated cinematic event, the new footage sets the stage for an unprecedented crossover as heroes from three different Earths are forced to band together to face total extinction.The upcoming blockbuster introduces a massive existential threat in the form of Doctor Doom, portrayed by returning Marvel veteran Robert Downey Jr. To combat the impending doom, the film officially assembles the Avengers, the X-Men, and the Fantastic Four on screen together for the very first time in Marvel's cinematic history. Adding to the massive scale, the project brings back Chris Evans as Steve Rogers alongside Hayley Atwell's Peggy Carter, abruptly interrupting the happily-ever-after ending established in 2019's Avengers: Endgame.Steering the massive ensemble are returning directors Joe and Anthony Russo, who previously shepherded Steve Rogers' arc from Captain America: The Winter Soldier through the conclusion of the Infinity Saga. The new film reframes Rogers' previous storybook ending as the catalyst for a brand new chapter. “We sort of played one beat past where Steve Rogers’ story ended with Peggy Carter,” Anthony Russo explained. “And in that moment, that's where Doomsday is born.”Avengers: Doomsday officially hits theaters everywhere on December 18.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Real-Life Sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning Unite on Screen in Sony's World War II Drama 'The Nightingale'
Entertainment.text: SummarySony has officially released the first look at its upcoming World War II drama film 'The Nightingale'Real-life siblings Dakota and Elle Fanning share the screen for the first time to portray sisters resisting the Nazi occupation in FranceThe highly anticipated adaptation of Kristin Hannah's best-selling novel arrives in theaters on March 19Sony has officially unveiled the trailer for The Nightingale, marking the very first time real-life sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning will share the screen together. Directed by Michael Morris, the highly anticipated cinematic adaptation of author Kristin Hannah's popular novel follows the siblings as they navigate survival and resistance in France during the World War II occupation by Nazi Germany.Taking on the complex lead roles, Elle Fanning plays Isabelle Rossignol, while Dakota Fanning portrays Vianne Mauriac. According to the film's official logline, the gripping narrative delivers a "powerful, emotional story of two sisters forced to embark on separate courageous, dangerous paths in a fight for survival and freedom during World War II." While the sisters previously both appeared in the 2001 film I Am Sam, Elle played an infant version of Dakota's character, meaning the two never actually acted opposite one another on camera.The star-studded historical ensemble cast also features Edmund Donovan, Shira Haas as Rachel de Champlain, Mark Rylance as Julien Rossignol, Albrecht Schuch, Douglas Hodge, Gwilym Lee, and Vinette Robinson. The screenplay was penned by Dana Stevens and Ann Peacock, with extensive production handled by the Fannings themselves alongside Reese Witherspoon, Brittany Kahan Ward, Lauren Neustadter, and Elizabeth Cantillon.The Nightingale will officially release in theaters on March 19.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Cherry Los Angeles' Holiday '26 Collection Is Made for the Long Way Home
Entertainment.text: Cherry Los Angeles is leaning into rugged Americana for its Holiday '26 collection, a winter range built around the kind of outdoor clothing that used to get handed down rather than replaced. The Los Angeles label focuses on hardwearing materials and careful construction, with pieces designed to look better the longer they're worn.Outerwear leads the collection, starting with shearling aviators and leather jackets cut from a leather Cherry developed in-house to soften and take on character over time. Stone-washed canvas work jackets offer a lighter option with a broken-in look from day one. Under those heavier pieces, hand-loomed alpaca sweaters and garment-dyed heavyweight hoodies handle the mid-layer.Thermals do much of the work in the rest of the range. The Best In The West, Ranchwear Boxy and Chevron Henley styles cover everything from western graphics to waffle-knit henleys, while the Frontier Henley Sherpa and Zip Up Sherpa Jacket add pile-lined warmth. Wide Leg Cargo Pants in Woodland Camo, a Plaid Western Shirt and an American Flag Knit Crew push the outdoorsman theme further. The women's lineup includes Knit Rugby shirts in Cabernet Red and Oatmeal, fitted T-shirts and eagle-graphic thermals.The palette stays grounded in workwear tones such as Vintage Black, Smoke, Faded Navy, Oatmeal and Cabernet Red, with bursts of orange and camo. A full run of 5 Star and American Truckers plus 5- and 6-panel caps finishes off the look.Cherry Los Angeles' Holiday '26 collection is available online and at Cherry stores.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Teenage Engineering Unveils the EP/BC-1 as Its First-Ever CD Player
Entertainment.text: SummaryTeenage Engineering has officially revealed the EP/BC-1, marking the brand's highly anticipated first venture into CD playersThe portable unit features a unique exposed disc design that resembles a traditional record player alongside advanced DJ capabilitiesPriced at $329 USD, the device is equipped with Bluetooth and Auracast streaming, beat detection, and the ability to rip CDs to digital filesTeenage Engineering has officially launched the EP/BC-1, marking the brand's very first foray into CD players. Serving as the inaugural entry in an entirely new "Broadcast Series" lineup, the portable device merges modern high-tech capabilities with a striking aesthetic that more closely resembles a traditional turntable than a standard compact disc player.Showcasing an exposed spinning disc on top of the device, the unit features built-in clips that allow it to seamlessly connect with recent Teenage Engineering products like the EP-35 portable speaker and the K.O. II groove machines. The sleek design is highlighted by a row of red LEDs that actively display left and right channel volume levels, alongside a dedicated box showing precise timecode and track-specific data.Beyond its striking visuals, the EP/BC-1 introduces advanced tools specifically geared toward DJs. A prominent varispeed dial allows users to speed up or slow down tracks for seamless beatmatching, supported by a built-in beat detection algorithm capable of outputting tempo in sync. Further modernizing the physical format, the USB-C-charged unit can directly rip audio CDs to digital files, stream via Bluetooth and Auracast, and includes a standard headphone jack for solo listening.The Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1 CD player is available for purchase now for $329 USD. Nonetheless, this remains an area of research interest.
